title: Entropy-influence inequalities for the planar percolation crossing event
statement: Conjecture 8. Let f represents the crossing event in planar percolation. Show that H(S(f)) = O(I(f)) and H(P(f)) = O(I(f)). (Here H is the entropy function.) [Context, PDF pp. 21-22: f is the indicator of a left-right crossing of an n by n box at p = 1/2; the spectral distribution S(f) gives a set S the probability f-hat(S)^2; the pivotality distribution P(f) gives S the probability that S is the set of pivotal variables; the first two moments of S and P agree; the first inequality is a special case of the entropy-influence conjecture of Friedgut and Kalai (1996), the second 'is not so general (it fails for the majority)'; I(f) is the total influence.]
status_search: Dedup: no entropy-influence or spectral-sample rows in intakes A-E. WebSearch 2026-09-08 (entropy influence conjecture status; Garban-Pete-Schramm spectral sample box estimates). The general Fourier-entropy-influence conjecture is open (Han, Combinatorica 2025, improved general bounds; further special classes verified in 2026); no paper on the percolation special case found. Kept.

attempt.method: Bound the entropy of a random subset S of the n x n box by a dyadic encoding: write pattern_k for the set of dyadic boxes of side n 2^{-k} that intersect S. By the chain rule H(S) = H(pattern_0) + sum_k H(pattern_{k+1} | pattern_k), and given pattern_k, pattern_{k+1} is determined by choosing, for each occupied box at level k, the nonempty subset of its four children that are occupied (15 possibilities), so H(pattern_{k+1} | pattern_k) <= (log 15) E[N_k] where N_k is the number of occupied boxes at level k. Hence H(S) <= log 2 + log 15 sum_k sum_{B at level k} P(S intersects B). This holds for ANY random set S; the entropy-influence question for a given f is therefore a question about the one-box marginals of the spectral sample at all scales.
attempt.result: For the percolation crossing event this reduces both inequalities to the box-intersection estimates of Garban, Pete and Schramm (Acta Math. 2010). For a box B of side r in the bulk, P(P(f) intersects B) is at most a constant times the four-arm probability alpha_4(r, n) (a pivotal in B needs four alternating arms from B to distance of order n), and, as I recall their first-moment section, they prove the same upper bound for the spectral sample, P(S(f) intersects B) <= C alpha_4(r, n); boxes touching the boundary have the half-plane three-arm bound (r/n)^2 and contribute at most O(1) per scale. With alpha_4(r,n) of order (r/n)^{5/4} on the triangular lattice, the level-k sum is (n/r)^2 (r/n)^{5/4} = (n/r)^{3/4} = 2^{3k/4}, a geometric series dominated by the finest scale, so sum_k sum_B P(S intersects B) <= C n^{3/4} <= C' I(f) since I(f) = n^2 alpha_4(1, n) is of order n^{3/4}. The same computation with the pivotal set gives H(P(f)) <= C I(f). If the recalled box estimate for the spectral sample is as stated (upper bound by a constant times the four-arm probability, uniformly over bulk boxes of all sizes r <= n), this settles both inequalities of Conjecture 8 on the triangular lattice, with constants; on Z^2 the same argument gives H = O(I(f)) as soon as the spectral-sample box estimate holds with any polynomial decay alpha_4(r,n) <= (r/n)^{1+delta}, which is what quasi-multiplicativity and the a priori bound alpha_4(r,n) <= C (r/n)^{1+delta} (from the five-arm exponent 2 and Reimer) give. I have not re-read Garban-Pete-Schramm to confirm the exact form of their one-box first-moment estimate; that check is the only thing between this argument and a proof, so the row is flagged as a partial result rather than a solution.
attempt.obstruction: The whole weight rests on the spectral-sample box estimate P(S intersects B) <= C alpha_4(r,n): the trivial first moment gives only P(S intersects B) <= E|S intersect B| = sum_{i in B} Inf_i(f), which is larger by a factor r^{3/4} and yields only the known general bound H(S) = O(I(f) log n). If Garban-Pete-Schramm's estimate is stated for boxes at distance at least r from the boundary only, the boundary boxes need the separate half-plane bound written above, which I did not verify in their paper.
attempt.key_identity: H(S) <= log 2 + log 15 sum_{scales k} sum_{dyadic boxes B at scale k} P(S intersects B) for any random set S; for the crossing event the box marginals decay like alpha_4(r,n), making the sum O(n^{3/4}) = O(I(f)).

locator: Conjecture 9 (Benjamini, Kalai, and Schramm 1999), Section 3.4.3, PDF p. 23
title: Noise stability of bounded-depth monotone threshold circuits
statement: Conjecture 9 (Benjamini, Kalai, and Schramm (1999)). (i) Let f be a Boolean function described by a monotone threshold circuit of size M and depth D. Then f is stable to (1/t)-noise where t = (log M)^{100D}. (ii) Let f be a monotone Boolean function described by a threshold circuit of size M and depth D. Then f is stable to (1/t)-noise where t = (log M)^{100D}. [The source adds: 'The constant 100 in the exponent is, of course, negotiable. In fact, replacing 100D with any function of D will be sufficient for most applications. The best we can hope for is that the conjectures are true if t behaves like t = (log M)^{D-1}. Part (i) is plausible but looks very difficult. Part (ii) is quite reckless and may well be false.' A monotone threshold circuit is built from weighted majority gates with nonnegative weights and no negations; 'stable to epsilon-noise' means P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) is small, where x^epsilon resamples each bit with probability epsilon.]
status_search: Dedup: no rows on Boolean circuit noise stability in intakes A-E (the campaign's noise rows are bootstrap percolation and Gaussian noise stability). WebSearch 2026-09-08 (Benjamini Kalai Schramm monotone threshold circuit noise stability conjecture): nothing found beyond the source and the 1999 paper. Kept.

attempt.method: Compare with what total influence gives. For any Boolean f and product noise, the hybrid argument gives P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) <= epsilon I(f). Boppana's theorem bounds I(f) <= C (log M)^{D-1} for monotone AND/OR circuits, so the AND/OR analogue of part (i) is immediate with t = (log M)^D. For threshold gates the influence route fails at depth one already: majority of M inputs has I = c sqrt(M) but is stable to 1/t-noise for every t -> infinity (Peres: linear threshold functions have noise sensitivity at most C sqrt(epsilon)). So part (i) is a statement about the Fourier tail beyond the influence, and it needs a composition principle for noise stability under monotone threshold gates.
attempt.result: Reduction of part (i) to a 'robust Peres theorem'. Feed a depth-D circuit bottom-up: at the first level each gate g_j is a linear threshold function of the inputs, and Peres gives P(g_j(x) != g_j(x^epsilon)) <= C sqrt(epsilon). At the second level a gate g receives inputs y = (g_j(x)) and y' = (g_j(x^epsilon)) which differ in each coordinate with probability at most C sqrt(epsilon), but the coordinates' disagreements are neither independent nor independent of y. If a linear threshold function satisfied P(g(y) != g(y')) <= C sqrt(max_j P(y_j != y'_j)) for every coupling of this kind, induction would give P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) <= C^D epsilon^{2^{-D}}, i.e. stability to 1/t-noise for t = t(D) -> infinity, which is qualitatively part (i) with a far worse dependence than (log M)^{100D}: the conjectured polylogarithmic t is then a quantitative statement that bounded-depth composition amplifies noise only polylogarithmically in the size. For general couplings the robust Peres statement is false (an adversary flips the largest-weight input), so the induction must use that the disagreements produced by the lower levels are 'random-like' with respect to g's weights, which is where the monotonicity and the polylogarithmic bound on influences of the lower gates should enter.
attempt.obstruction: There is no composition theorem for noise stability of threshold gates with dependent input noise, and the known techniques (hypercontractivity for the Fourier tail, Peres' argument for a single gate, Boppana/Hastad influence bounds for AND/OR) each break at the second level of threshold gates; part (ii) additionally allows negative weights inside a monotone function, for which no structural result exists at all, consistent with the source calling it reckless.
attempt.key_identity: P(f(x) != f(x^epsilon)) <= epsilon I(f) for any f (hybrid argument), which settles the AND/OR analogue via Boppana but not the threshold case, where majority has I of order sqrt(M) yet is stable.

locator: Conjecture 10 (Benjamini, Kalai, and Schramm 1999), Section 3.4.4, PDF p. 24
title: Reverse Hastad: approximation by bounded-depth circuits of size governed by the total influence
statement: Conjecture 10 (Benjamini, Kalai, and Schramm (1999)). For some absolute constant C the following holds. A Boolean function f can be 0.01-approximated by a circuit of depth d of size M where (log M)^{Cd} >= I(f). [The source calls this 'the reverse Hastad conjecture', after Theorem 3.20(ii): if f is described by a depth D size M Boolean circuit then I(f) <= C (log M)^{D-1}. Reading: for every f and every d, f is 0.01-approximable by a depth-d circuit whose size M satisfies (log M)^{Cd} >= I(f), i.e. of size exp(I(f)^{1/(Cd)}).]
status_search: Dedup: not in intakes A-E. WebSearch 2026-09-08 (reverse Hastad conjecture Benjamini Kalai Schramm): nothing beyond the 1999 paper and this survey. Kept.

attempt.method: Calibrate the statement against known functions. Parity on k variables has I = k and, by Hastad's lower bound, needs size exp(c k^{1/(d-1)}) in depth d, so any C >= 1 is consistent and C < 1 is excluded: the conjecture says parity is the hardest function for its influence. Majority on n bits has I of order sqrt(n) and is 0.01-approximable by depth-2 circuits (DNF) of size exp(O(sqrt(n))), i.e. log M of order I(f), consistent. Friedgut's junta theorem gives, for every f with I(f) = k, a 0.01-approximating junta on exp(O(k)) variables, hence a depth-2 circuit of size exp(exp(O(k))): this proves the conjecture with log M replaced by log log M, a doubly exponential loss, and shows the conjecture is a strengthening of Friedgut's theorem at depth 2: every function of influence k is close to a DNF of size exp(k^{O(1)}), not just to a junta on exp(O(k)) variables.
attempt.result: At depth d = 2 the conjecture is equivalent to: every Boolean f with I(f) = k is 0.01-close to a DNF of size exp(k^{C'}). Known: Friedgut's junta is a function of exp(O(k)) variables and can be written as a DNF of size exp(exp(O(k))); a monotone f with I(f) = k is close to a function of exp(O(k)) variables with the same influence bound, and the question is whether the junta's own structure can be exploited. Test case: the 'tribes' function (a DNF with terms of size log n - log log n) has I of order log n and is itself a DNF of size n = exp(O(I)), consistent. A candidate counterexample must have small influence and no small DNF approximation: address/multiplexer-type functions have influence O(log n) and DNF size polynomial in n = exp(O(I)), again consistent. I found no candidate violating exp(k^{C'}) at depth 2, and the depth-d version reduces to depth 2 only if one accepts a loss in the exponent, so the conjecture is plausible and unresolved.
attempt.obstruction: The junta theorem is the only general structural consequence of small total influence, and it loses an exponential; bridging exp(exp(O(k))) and exp(k^{O(1)}) needs an approximation theory for bounded-depth circuits driven by Fourier concentration at low levels (small influence implies most spectral weight at levels <= O(k)), and low-degree Fourier concentration is known to give bounded-depth approximators only for functions that are already in AC0 (Linial-Mansour-Nisan is the converse direction).
attempt.key_identity: Parity shows C >= 1 is necessary; Friedgut's junta theorem gives the conjecture with a doubly exponential size at depth 2.

locator: Section 3.3.4 (a problem of Benjamini and Brieussel), PDF p. 22
title: Noise sensitivity of simple random walk on Liouville Cayley graphs
statement: [Verbatim from the source, Section 3.3.4.] Consider n steps simple random walk (SRW) X_n on a Cayley graph of a finitely generated infinite group Gamma. Refresh independently each step with probability epsilon, to get Y_n from X_n. Are there groups for which the positions at time n, X_n and Y_n are asymptotically independent? That is, the l_1 (total variation) distance between the chain (X_n, Y_n) and two independent copies (X'_n, X''_n) is going to 0, with n. Note that on the line Z, they are uniformally correlated, and therefore also on any group with a non trivial homomorphism to R, or any group that has a finite index subgroup with a non trivial homomorphism to R. On the free group and for any non-Liouville group, X_n and Y_n are correlated as well, but for a different reason: Both X_n and Y_n have nontrivial correlation with X_1. Itai Benjamini and Jeremie Brieussel conjecture that these are the only ways not to be noise sensitive. That is, if a Cayley graph is Liouville and the group does not have a finite index subgroup with a homomorphism to the reals, then the Cayley graph is noise sensitive for the simple random walk. In particular, the Grigorchuk group is noise sensitive for the simple random walk!
status_search: Dedup: not in intakes A-E (Liouville rows there concern Liouville quantum gravity). WebSearch 2026-09-08 (Benjamini Brieussel noise sensitivity random walks on groups). STATUS: the conjecture has since been refined by its authors: Benjamini and Brieussel, 'Noise sensitivity of random walks on groups' (arXiv 1901.03617, ALEA 2023) define l^1-noise sensitivity (the total variation statement above) and entropy noise sensitivity, prove that either property forces the Liouville property, that homomorphisms to free abelian groups obstruct l^1-noise sensitivity, and give examples of l^1 and entropy noise sensitive walks; they conjecture that (G, mu) is entropy noise sensitive iff it is Liouville and believe l^1-noise sensitivity implies entropy noise sensitivity. Later work: Kalai-Kozma? no; 'Non-noise sensitivity for word hyperbolic groups' (2022), 'Noise stability on hyperbolic groups' (2025), 'Noise sensitivity on affine Weyl groups' (2024). The Grigorchuk group statement and the l^1 conjecture as stated here remain open as far as I found. Kept.

attempt.method: Write X_n = g_1 ... g_n and Y_n = g'_1 ... g'_n where g'_i = g_i off the resampled set R (a Bernoulli(epsilon) subset of {1, ..., n}) and independent otherwise. The two necessary conditions are visible from this: a homomorphism phi: Gamma -> Z gives phi(X_n) - phi(Y_n) = sum_{i in R} (phi(g_i) - phi(g'_i)), a sum of about epsilon n independent terms, while phi(X_n) itself has variance of order n, so (phi(X_n), phi(Y_n)) has correlation 1 - epsilon in the limit; and if the Poisson boundary is nontrivial the first steps bias both endpoints toward the same boundary point. The conjecture says nothing else can correlate the endpoints.
attempt.result: A reduction to a finite-n entropy statement. Let H_n = H(X_n) be the entropy of the walk and consider H(X_n | (g_i)_{i not in R}), the residual entropy of the endpoint given the shared increments. Total variation independence of (X_n, Y_n) implies I(X_n ; Y_n) -> 0, and since Y_n is a function of the shared increments and independent extra ones, I(X_n ; Y_n) <= I(X_n ; (g_i)_{i not in R}) = H_n - H(X_n | shared increments). So l^1-noise sensitivity requires H(X_n | shared increments) = H_n - o(1): resampling an epsilon-fraction of the steps must destroy essentially all information about the endpoint, which for Liouville groups (H_n = o(n)) is a statement about how the sublinear entropy is distributed along the word. In the abelian case the shared increments determine X_n up to the sum of epsilon n independent steps, whose entropy is of order log(epsilon n), while H_n is of order log n: the residual entropy is H_n - O(1)... which is why abelian groups fail only at the level of the normalised position, not of entropy; this is exactly why Benjamini-Brieussel separate the l^1 and entropy notions. For the Grigorchuk group the walk entropy grows like n^{alpha} with alpha < 1 (Erschler-type bounds), and the conjecture predicts that conjugation by the shared prefixes scrambles the resampled increments enough that no O(1) statistic of X_n survives.
attempt.obstruction: All known tools for Liouville groups (entropy criterion, Poisson boundary triviality) are asymptotic and insensitive to an epsilon-fraction of the increments; a proof of noise sensitivity needs a quantitative mixing statement for the 'shared-increment' sigma-field at finite n, and no such technique exists even for the simplest intermediate-growth examples. The obstruction from Z-quotients shows that any proof must use the absence of virtual homomorphisms to Z, a purely algebraic condition whose probabilistic meaning (beyond the CLT along the homomorphism) is not understood.
attempt.key_identity: I(X_n ; Y_n) <= H(X_n) - H(X_n | (g_i)_{i not in R}); l^1-noise sensitivity forces the shared increments to carry o(1) information about the endpoint.

title: Noise sensitivity of the event that the first-passage distance exceeds its median
statement: [Verbatim from the source, Section 3.3.3.] Consider an infinite planar grid where every edge is assigned a length: 1 with probability 1/2 and 2 with probability 1/2 (independently). This model of a random metric on the planar grid is called first-passage percolation. An old question is to understand what is the variance V(n) of the distance D from (0,0) to (n,0)? Now, let M be the median value of D and consider the Boolean function f describing the event 'D >= M'. Is f noise sensitive? Benjamini, Kalai and Schramm (2003) showed, more or less, that f is sensitive to logarithmic level of noise, and concluded that V(n) = O(n/log n). (The argument uses hypercontractivity and is similar to the argument for critical planar percolation.) To show that f is sensitive to noise level of n^delta for delta > 0 would imply that V(n) = O(n^{1-c}). A very interesting question is whether methods used for critical planar percolation for obtaining stronger noise sensitivity results can also be applied here.
status_search: Dedup: the campaign's FPP rows (Chatterjee 2017 lower-bound problems, the Auffinger-Damron-Hanson survey) concern variance bounds and geodesics, not the noise sensitivity of the above-median event. WebSearch 2026-09-08 (first passage percolation noise sensitivity above median). STATUS: the question is attributed to Benjamini (2011) and is open: Ahlberg-Deijfen-Sfragara, 'Chaos, concentration and multiple valleys in first-passage percolation' (2023) prove chaos of the geodesic under resampling; 'Is being above the median a noise sensitive property?' (arXiv 2308.16388) answers YES for passage times of paths with constrained vertical fluctuation, not the full model; 'Noise sensitivity and variance lower bound for minimal left-right crossing of a square in FPP' (arXiv 2505.03211). The polynomial-noise question for D itself remains open. Kept.

attempt.method: Separate the two notions the question conflates: (a) noise sensitivity at fixed epsilon (Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm criterion sum_e Inf_e(f)^2 -> 0), and (b) sensitivity at polynomial noise epsilon = n^{-delta}, which is what would improve the variance bound. Both are statements about the Fourier spectrum of f = 1{D >= M}: (a) says the spectral sample S_f has |S_f| -> infinity in probability, (b) says |S_f| >= n^{delta} with probability 1 - o(1), and by the BKS argument Var(D) <= C n / (typical spectral level), roughly.
attempt.result: The influence of an edge e on f is at most P(e lies on a geodesic) times P(a unit change of D crosses the median | e on the geodesic) <= C (1/n)-ish times n^{-chi} where n^{chi} is the scale of the fluctuations of D, using that geodesics have n^{1+o(1)} edges spread over the corridor; so sum_e Inf_e^2 <= n^{1+2xi} (n^{-1-chi})^2 -> 0 where n^{xi} is the transversal fluctuation scale (2 xi = chi + 1 under the KPZ relation predicts 1 + 4/3 - 2 - 2/3 < 0), which gives (a) once the a priori bounds P(e on geodesic) <= n^{-1+o(1)} on average and Var(D) >= n^{2chi} with chi > 0 are available; the second is not known (Var(D) >= c log n is the only lower bound), so even (a) is conditional. For (b), a KPZ heuristic predicts the spectral level: D is a sum of order n^{1/3} approximately independent contributions from corridor segments of length n^{2/3}, each with O(n^{1/3}) fluctuations, so f = 1{D >= M} should behave like a majority-type function of n^{1/3} nearly independent blocks, each block being itself a function of n^{2/3 + 2 xi} edges; majority of m independent bits has spectral level of order... its spectral sample is of size O(1) with probability bounded below, so the above-median function is expected to be noise STABLE at the block level and sensitive only through the internal structure of the blocks: the prediction is sensitivity at noise level epsilon = n^{-delta} for some delta > 0 iff within a block of length n^{2/3} the passage time is polynomially noise sensitive, a self-similar reduction with no base case.
attempt.obstruction: Every quantitative tool (hypercontractivity/BKS, randomised algorithms as in Schramm-Steif) needs either a bound on the largest influence at polynomial scale or a randomised algorithm that computes f while querying each edge with polynomially small probability; for the crossing event such an algorithm exists (exploration path), for D there is no known algorithm that determines D >= M without examining a positive fraction of the corridor with probability bounded below, which is exactly the localisation of geodesics that is not controlled beyond n^{1/2+o(1)}... (transversal fluctuation upper bounds are only known at that level), so the method that worked for percolation has no known analogue here.
attempt.key_identity: BKS: Var(D) <= C sum_e Inf_e(D)^2 / (typical spectral level); noise sensitivity at level n^{-delta} would give Var(D) = O(n^{1-c}).

title: One-value concentration of the chromatic number of the sparse random graph
statement: Conjecture: There exists a sequence d_k : k >= 2 such that w.h.p. chi(G_{n,d/n}) = k for d_{k-1} < d < d_k. Friedgut (1999), Achlioptas and Friedgut (1999) came close to proving this. [Same source, PDF pp. 83-84: Luczak (1991): w.h.p. chi(G_{n,d/n}) takes one of two values; Achlioptas and Naor (2005): with k_d the smallest integer k >= 2 with d < 2k log k, w.h.p. chi is k_d or k_d + 1.]
status_search: Dedup: no chromatic-number rows in intakes A-E. WebSearch 2026-09-08 (chromatic number sparse random graph one value conjecture status): Coja-Oghlan and Vilenchik ('Chasing the k-colorability threshold', 2013, and later work) determine chi(G(n, d/n)) for all d in a set of asymptotic density one, and the k-colorability threshold is known up to an additive o_k(1) for large k; for random regular graphs Coja-Oghlan, Efthymiou and Hetterich (2016) determine the threshold exactly for large k; the existence of the limit d_k for every fixed k (in particular k = 3) is still open. Kept.

attempt.method: Split the conjecture into sharpness and convergence. Achlioptas-Friedgut give a sharp threshold: for each k there are d_k(n) with P(chi <= k) jumping from o(1) to 1 - o(1) in a window of width o(1) around d_k(n). So the conjecture is exactly the statement that lim_n d_k(n) exists for every k, the same 'convergence of the threshold sequence' question as for random k-SAT.
attempt.result: For k large the limit exists and is known: Coja-Oghlan-Vilenchik pin the threshold to within o_k(1), and for random regular graphs Coja-Oghlan-Efthymiou-Hetterich identify it exactly (as the condensation/one-step-replica-symmetry-breaking prediction) for k >= k_0; on G(n, d/n) the exact identification for large k follows the same route (the 'cavity' formula) and I believe is done in the same line of work, which would make the conjecture true for k >= k_0 and open for small k, with k = 3 (predicted d_3 = 4.687...) the first open case. For small k the available bounds sandwich the threshold in an interval of positive length (e.g. for k = 3, between 4.03 and 4.937 by second-moment and first-moment arguments), and the second moment method, which gave Achlioptas-Naor's two values, provably cannot reach the exact threshold because of the condensation transition below it.
attempt.obstruction: Convergence of d_k(n) requires identifying the limit, and for small k the limit is predicted by a replica-symmetry-breaking formula whose rigorous derivation needs the full condensation picture (Bapst, Coja-Oghlan, Hetterich, Rassmann, Vilenchik for large k) at small k, where the 1-RSB prediction is believed exact but the proof techniques (contiguity and planted-model arguments) rely on large-k expansions.
attempt.key_identity: Achlioptas-Friedgut sharpness reduces the conjecture to the existence of lim_n d_k(n); for k >= k_0 the limit is the condensation-threshold formula.

locator: Hamilton cycles slide, PDF p. 166 (with pp. 167-170)
title: Hamiltonicity of the random graph with minimum degree three above edge density three halves
statement: We now consider conditioning on minimum degree at least three. Let L_c = lim_{n -> infinity} Pr(G_{n,cn;3} is Hamiltonian). Conjecture: L_c = 1 for all c >= 3/2. [Following slides: conjecture true for c = 3/2 (Robinson and Wormald 1984, the random cubic graph); Bollobas, Cooper, Fenner, Frieze (2000): L_c = 1 for c >= 128; Frieze (2012): L_c = 1 for c >= 10; 'Conjecture true for c >= 3, assuming numerical solution of some differential equations'. Here G_{n,m;3} is uniform over graphs with n vertices, m edges and minimum degree at least 3.]
status_search: Dedup: no Hamiltonicity rows in intakes A-E. WebSearch 2026-09-08 (Hamilton cycles random graphs minimum degree at least three Anastos Frieze): Anastos and Frieze, 'Hamilton cycles in random graphs with minimum degree at least 3: an improved analysis' (RSA 2020) prove L_c = 1 for c > 2.662..., matching the Frieze-Pittel bound for Posa set expansion; the conjectured threshold 3/2 remains open. Kept.

attempt.method: Identify why c = 3/2 is the natural boundary: 2m >= 3n forces c >= 3/2, and at c = 3/2 exactly the graph is a random cubic graph, Hamiltonian w.h.p. by Robinson-Wormald's small-subgraph-conditioning second moment computation. For c slightly above 3/2 the degree sequence of G_{n,cn;3} is a truncated Poisson (conditioned to be >= 3) with mean 2c, so the graph is a random graph with a given degree sequence whose maximum degree is of order log n / log log n.
attempt.result: Reduction: the conjecture follows from Hamiltonicity w.h.p. of the configuration-model random graph with the truncated-Poisson degree sequence of mean 2c, for every c > 3/2, by contiguity of G_{n,cn;3} with that model; for degree sequences with minimum degree 3 and BOUNDED maximum degree, Hamiltonicity w.h.p. is known (Cooper-Frieze-Reed 2002 for regular and near-regular, via the Robinson-Wormald method), and the only obstacle for the truncated-Poisson sequence is the unbounded maximum degree. So the conjecture is equivalent to extending the Robinson-Wormald second-moment/small-subgraph-conditioning computation for the number of Hamilton cycles to degree sequences with maximum degree of order log n / log log n, which is where the variance of the number of Hamilton cycles picks up contributions from the high-degree vertices that the current computations cannot control.
attempt.obstruction: The Posa-rotation approach of Frieze and Anastos-Frieze is capped at c = 2.662 by the expansion properties of 2-matchings, and the second-moment approach has never been carried out with unbounded degrees; a proof for c in (3/2, 2.662] needs one of the two to be pushed beyond its known limit, and the second is the natural one given that the c = 3/2 case is exactly Robinson-Wormald.
attempt.key_identity: At c = 3/2 the model is the random cubic graph (Robinson-Wormald); above it the model is contiguous with a configuration model with a truncated-Poisson degree sequence of unbounded maximum degree.

title: Existence of the random k-SAT satisfiability threshold for every k
statement: Random k-SAT. Conjecture: there exists c_k such that if m = cn then lim_{n -> infinity} Pr(I is satisfiable) = 1 for c < c_k and 0 for c > c_k. Friedgut (1999) has come close to proving this. Conjecture is true for k = 2. It is known that c_2 = 1. [I is a random k-CNF formula with n variables and m clauses, each clause a uniformly random set of k literals on distinct variables.]
status_search: Dedup: no k-SAT rows in intakes A-E. Status (known to me, not re-searched): Ding, Sly and Sun, 'Proof of the satisfiability conjecture for large k' (STOC 2015; Ann. Math. 2022) prove the conjecture, with c_k given by the one-step replica symmetry breaking formula, for all k >= k_0 with k_0 a large absolute constant; Friedgut's theorem gives a sharp threshold sequence c_k(n) for every k; for 3 <= k < k_0 the existence of the limit is open (for k = 3 the rigorous bounds are roughly 3.52 <= liminf and limsup <= 4.49, the prediction being 4.2667). Kept for k < k_0.

attempt.method: As for the chromatic number: Friedgut's sharp threshold theorem reduces the conjecture to the convergence of the threshold sequence c_k(n) defined by P(satisfiable) = 1/2, and convergence has only ever been proved by identifying the limit.
attempt.result: For k >= k_0 the limit is the 1-RSB prediction (Ding-Sly-Sun), proved through the survey-propagation/condensation structure of the solution space, which is rigorous only when k is large enough for the 'frozen variables' picture to be established by first and second moment computations with large-k expansions. For small k the same formula is believed exact, and the proof would need the same structural statements (the solution space is a union of well-separated clusters with frozen variables above the condensation threshold) without the large-k expansions; for k = 3 the second moment method fails already at c of order 2^k ln 2 - O(k), far below the predicted threshold, because of the condensation transition. A different route to mere existence of the limit (without its value) would be a monotonicity or self-averaging argument in n, which does not exist: Friedgut's sharpness gives the window but not the location, and the location can in principle oscillate.
attempt.obstruction: The Ding-Sly-Sun argument uses k large in essentially every estimate (moment computations of clusters, contiguity of the planted model); nobody has a technique that proves convergence of a threshold sequence without computing it, and the computation for k = 3 requires the 1-RSB machinery to be controlled at small k where the physics prediction, though believed, has no rigorous foundation.
attempt.key_identity: Friedgut sharpness + Ding-Sly-Sun for large k; the open content is lim_n c_k(n) for 3 <= k < k_0.

title: The Beardwood-Halton-Hammersley constant
statement: Open Questions/Problems. Determine the constant beta in the Beardwood, Halton and Hammersley theorem. [The BHH theorem: for n i.i.d. uniform points in the unit square the length of the shortest tour through them satisfies L_n / sqrt(n) -> beta almost surely, for a constant beta = beta_2 whose value is not known; numerical estimates put beta_2 near 0.7124, with rigorous bounds 0.625 <= beta_2 <= 0.9204.]
status_search: Dedup: intakes A-E carry the variance (E0030) and distributional (E0041) questions for the TSP tour length, not the value of the constant. Status (known to me, not re-searched): no closed form is known or expected; the best rigorous bounds are Steinerberger's lower bound 0.625 (2015) and the upper bound 0.9204; numerical estimate 0.7124 (Applegate, Bixby, Chvatal, Cook). Kept.

attempt.method: Ask what 'determine' can mean. beta_2 = lim E L_n/sqrt(n) is, by the Aldous-Steele objective method, the expected per-point length of an optimal 'infinite tour' of the unit-intensity Poisson process if such a translation-invariant local limit of optimal tours exists; the constant would then be an expectation over a translation-invariant random structure on the Poisson process, for which a closed form is not expected. So the realistic content of the problem is (a) existence and description of the local limit of optimal tours, and (b) sharper rigorous bounds.
attempt.result: (a) is itself open: it is not known that the optimal tours on n points converge locally (in the Aldous-Steele sense) to a translation-invariant infinite path on the Poisson process, nor that such a limit is unique; the analogous statement for the minimal spanning tree is known (it converges to the Poisson MSF, single tree or not being a separate open question already in the campaign as C0113). If (a) held, beta_2 = E[half the sum of the two edge lengths at the origin of the limit tour] by mass transport, and the bounds in (b) would become questions about the local structure of the limit. (b): the lower bound 0.625 comes from comparing with the minimal matching/nearest-neighbour graph (each point has two tour edges each at least the nearest-neighbour distance, with a refinement for the second edge), and the upper bound from explicit constructions (space-filling curve heuristics improved by local optimisation); improving either needs a structural property of optimal tours, e.g. the distribution of the angle between the two tour edges at a point, which is unknown.
attempt.obstruction: The optimal tour has no local characterisation (unlike the MST, which is determined locally by the cycle criterion), so every known tool gives only bounds; exact determination would need an unexpected exact solvability, and there is no evidence for it.
attempt.key_identity: beta_2 = E[per-point length of the local limit of optimal tours] if the local limit exists (objective method); the lower bound uses that both tour edges at a point are at least the nearest-neighbour distance.

title: Asymptotics of the random three-dimensional assignment problem
statement: Open Questions/Problems. Determine the asymptotics for the value of a random multi-dimensional assignment problem and find asymptotically optimal heuristics. Give a uniform [0,1] weight X_e to each edge of the complete 3-uniform hypergraph H_{n:3}. Let Z_n denote the minimum weight of a perfect matching. It is known that w.h.p. c_1/n <= Z_n <= c_2 log n / n. The LHS is easy. The RHS depends on a deep result of Johansson, Kahn and Vu (2008). [H_{n:3} is the complete 3-partite 3-uniform hypergraph with parts of size n, so a perfect matching is a three-dimensional axial assignment; the two-dimensional version is the random assignment problem with limit zeta(2) (Aldous).]
status_search: Dedup: intakes A-E carry the two-dimensional random assignment rows (Parisi formula, variance, fluctuation lower bound); the three-dimensional problem is not there. WebSearch 2026-09-08 (random 3-dimensional assignment minimum weight perfect matching 3-uniform hypergraph asymptotics): the only rigorous bounds found are those on the slide (the upper bound via Johansson-Kahn-Vu's hypergraph matching threshold); no determination of the order of Z_n. Kept.

attempt.method: Compare the two bounds with the two-dimensional case to see which is the truth. Lower bound: each of the n matching edges costs at least the minimum of the n^2 weights at one of its vertices, giving Z_n >= c/n. Upper bound: keep only edges of weight at most p = C log n / n^2, i.e. a random 3-uniform hypergraph with about n^3 p = C n log n edges, which by Johansson-Kahn-Vu has a perfect matching w.h.p., so Z_n <= n p = C log n / n. In two dimensions the analogous bounds are c/n <= Z_n <= C log n/n... times n, and the truth, Aldous's zeta(2), sits at the LOWER bound's order: the optimal matching uses edges cheaper on average than the threshold edges. So the natural conjecture is Z_n = Theta(1/n), and more precisely that n Z_n converges to a constant c_3 given by a recursive distributional equation on the local weak limit of the weighted hypergraph.
attempt.result: The objective-method reduction: rescaling weights by n^2, the neighbourhood of a vertex in H_{n:3} with weights n^2 X_e converges to a Poisson-weighted infinite hypertree (each vertex has a Poisson process of rate 1 of incident edges, each edge having two other vertices with their own independent hypertrees). If the minimum-weight perfect matching converges locally to an invariant perfect matching of this limit object (the analogue of Aldous's zeta(2) argument), then lim n Z_n = c_3 = E[weight of the edge covering the root]/3 and c_3 is characterised by the recursive distributional equation for the 'cost of not matching the root': X = min_e (w_e - Y_e^{(1)} - Y_e^{(2)}) over the Poisson edges at the root with Y independent copies of X (two subtrees per edge instead of one), the three-dimensional analogue of the logistic RDE whose solution gives zeta(2). Writing the RDE and checking whether it has a unique solution with the right tail (the two-dimensional solution is logistic) is the concrete next step; the answer would give Z_n = (c_3 + o(1))/n, refuting the log n upper bound as the truth.
attempt.obstruction: Aldous's zeta(2) proof needs (i) endogeny/uniqueness for the RDE and (ii) a local-convergence argument that the finite optimal matching is close to the limit matching, using the bipartite graph structure (alternating paths); for hypergraph matchings there is no alternating-path augmentation structure, so (ii) has no known proof strategy, and even the existence of the limit c_3 is open.
attempt.key_identity: Objective-method RDE: X = min over Poisson edges of (w - Y^{(1)} - Y^{(2)}), the three-dimensional analogue of the logistic RDE of the random assignment problem.
